newsitem.title: USA: Arizona killer put to death.
newsitem.headline: Arizona killer put to death.

text.p: Protesting his innocence to the end, convicted killer William Lyle Woratzeck was put to death early Wednesday for the 1980 murder of a mentally-impaired woman, prison officials said.
Officials said Woratzeck, 51, died at 12:12 a.m. (2:12 EDT) at the state prison complex after being administered a lethal injection while strapped to a table.
"I want the state of Arizona to know they are executing an innocent man. Tell my wife that I love her and tell the rest of my family that I love them," he told onlookers.
Woratzeck was the eighth person to be put to death in Arizona since the state resumed capital punishment in 1992 after a 29-year absence. The last execution was in January.
Woratzeck, who was sentenced to death in October 1980 after a five-day jury trial, spent his last day meeting with a brother, neice and nephew inside the death house at the prison.
His last meal consisted of a sirloin steak, french fries, onion rings, shrimp and cherry cheese cake, soda and coffee.
Several last-minute appeals were denied late Tuesday.
Woratzeck was convicted of killing Linda Louise Leslie, a 36-year-old suffering from Huntington's disease who had rented an apartment from him in Casa Grande, Ariz.
Authorities said Woratzeck broke into Leslie's room in the small southern Arizona community in the early morning hours of March 6, 1980.
Prosecutors said he then beat her with a hammer, stabbed her three times and strangled her. He set the residence on fire, but not before robbing Leslie of $107, they said.
Woratzeck was arrested one week later for breaking into a nursery. While in jail, he was charged with Leslie's murder and other offences.
An appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals was denied last September and the U.S. Supreme Court in April also refused to grant him reconsideration.
To the end, Woratzeck's relatives claimed he did not commit the murder.
Woratzeck's attorneys also maintained his innocence but said that even if he did kill Leslie, the crime did not warrant the death penalty.
